theorySlides.title: What is OOP? 🏗️
theorySlides.content:
Object-Oriented Programming organizes code into objects - bundles of data and functionality.

Key concepts:
• **Class**: A blueprint for creating objects
• **Object**: An instance of a class
• **Attributes**: Data stored in an object
• **Methods**: Functions that belong to an object

theorySlides.title: Why Use OOP? 💡
theorySlides.content:
Benefits of OOP:

✅ **Modularity** - Code is organized into self-contained units
✅ **Reusability** - Create once, use many times
✅ **Maintainability** - Easy to update and fix
✅ **Real-world modeling** - Objects represent real things

theorySlides.title: Creating a Class
theorySlides.content: Use the class keyword to define a blueprint.

theorySlides.title: The self Parameter 🔑
theorySlides.content:
**self** refers to the current instance of the class.

It allows you to:
• Access attributes: self.name
• Call methods: self.bark()
• Distinguish instance from class variables

questions.question: What is __init__ used for?
questions.explanation: __init__ is the constructor that sets up initial state when an object is created.

questions.question: What does "self" refer to?
questions.explanation: self refers to the current instance of the class being created or used.

questions.question: How do you create an object from class Dog?
questions.explanation: In Python, you create objects by calling the class name like a function: Dog()

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.description: Learn how to reuse code with class inheritance

theorySlides.title: What is Inheritance? 🌳
theorySlides.content:
Inheritance allows a class to inherit attributes and methods from another class.

Terminology:
• **Parent/Base class**: The class being inherited from
• **Child/Derived class**: The class that inherits
• **Override**: Replace parent method in child

theorySlides.title: Why Inheritance? 🎯
theorySlides.content:
Benefits:

✅ **DRY** - Don't Repeat Yourself
✅ **Hierarchy** - Model real relationships
✅ **Extend** - Add features without changing original
✅ **Polymorphism** - Same interface, different behavior

theorySlides.title: Creating Child Classes
theorySlides.content: Pass the parent class in parentheses.

theorySlides.title: Using super() 🦸
theorySlides.content: super() calls the parent class methods.

questions.question: What does super() do?
questions.explanation: super() allows calling methods from the parent class.

questions.question: How do you create a child class?
questions.explanation: In Python, put the parent class name in parentheses: class Child(Parent)

questions.question: What is method overriding?
questions.explanation: Override means defining a method in child class with same name as parent to replace behavior.

theorySlides.title: List Comprehensions ✨
theorySlides.content:
List comprehensions provide a concise way to create lists.

Syntax: [expression for item in iterable]
With filter: [expression for item in iterable if condition]

theorySlides.title: Why List Comprehensions? 🚀
theorySlides.content:
Benefits:

✅ **Readable** - Clear intent in one line
✅ **Fast** - More efficient than loops
✅ **Pythonic** - The "Python way"
✅ **Flexible** - Filter and transform together

theorySlides.title: Basic Examples
theorySlides.content: Transform and filter data in one line.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
# Squares of 1-5
squares = [x**2 for x in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)  # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

# Even numbers only
evens = [x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]
print(evens)  # [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]

theorySlides.title: Nested Comprehensions 🔄
theorySlides.content: Create 2D structures or flatten lists.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
# Flatten a 2D list
matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]
flat = [num for row in matrix for num in row]
print(flat)  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

# Create multiplication table
table = [[i*j for j in range(1,4)] for i in range(1,4)]
# [[1,2,3], [2,4,6], [3,6,9]]

questions.question: What does [x for x in range(5) if x > 2] return?
questions.explanation: Only values greater than 2 pass the filter: 3 and 4.

questions.question: Which is equivalent to: result = []; for x in items: result.append(x*2)?
questions.explanation: List comprehension syntax: [expression for item in iterable]

codingChallenge.title: Squares of Evens
codingChallenge.description: Create list of squares of even numbers from 1 to 10.
codingChallenge.starterCode:
# Create squares of even numbers 1-10
# Expected: [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]
squares = # Your code
print(squares)
codingChallenge.solution:

theorySlides.title: Lambda Functions ⚡
theorySlides.content:
Lambda functions are small anonymous functions.

Syntax: lambda args: expression

Perfect for short, one-time functions.

theorySlides.title: Lambda vs Regular Functions 🆚
theorySlides.content:
Comparison:

**Regular function:**
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

**Lambda function:**
add = lambda a, b: a + b

Use lambda for simple, single-use operations.

theorySlides.title: Lambda with sorted()
theorySlides.content: Sort with custom keys.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
students = [("Alice", 85), ("Bob", 92), ("Charlie", 78)]

# Sort by grade (second element)
sorted_students = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1])
print(sorted_students)

theorySlides.title: Lambda with map() & filter() 🔧
theorySlides.content: Use lambda with functional programming tools.
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Double each number
doubled = list(map(lambda x: x*2, numbers))
# [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

# Keep only evens
evens = list(filter(lambda x: x%2==0, numbers))
# [2, 4]

questions.question: Correct lambda to add two numbers?
What can lambda functions contain?
questions.explanation: Lambda functions can only contain a single expression, not multiple statements.

questions.question: What does map(lambda x: x**2, [1,2,3]) return?
questions.explanation: map() applies the lambda to each element: 1²=1, 2²=4, 3²=9

codingChallenge.title: Sort by Length
codingChallenge.description: Sort words by length using lambda.
codingChallenge.starterCode:
words = ["python", "is", "awesome"]
# Sort by length
result = sorted(words, key=# your lambda)
print(result)
codingChallenge.solution:
words = ["python", "is", "awesome"]
result = sorted(words, key=lambda w: len(w))
print(result)

theorySlides.title: Try/Except 🛡️
theorySlides.content:
Handle errors without crashing your program.

Common exceptions:
• ValueError - wrong value type
• TypeError - wrong operation on type
• ZeroDivisionError - divide by zero
• FileNotFoundError - missing file

theorySlides.title: Why Handle Exceptions? 💡
theorySlides.content:
Benefits:

✅ **Graceful failure** - App doesn't crash
✅ **User-friendly** - Show helpful error messages
✅ **Recovery** - Try alternative approaches
✅ **Logging** - Track errors for debugging

theorySlides.title: Basic Syntax
theorySlides.content: Wrap risky code in try/except.

theorySlides.title: Multiple Exceptions 🎯
theorySlides.content: Handle different errors differently.

questions.question: Which block always runs?
questions.explanation: finally always executes, regardless of exceptions.

questions.question: How do you catch ANY exception?
questions.explanation: A bare "except:" catches all exceptions (though "except Exception:" is preferred).

questions.question: What does "raise" do?
questions.explanation: raise creates and throws an exception that can be caught by try/except.
